summary: Russian Hill was too steep to use, and the record starts with the city cutting it down. In 1916 the grade of Larkin Street between Chestnut and Francisco was reduced from 29 per cent to 16, at the property owners' own request; Francisco Street above it was reported "practically inaccessible", and the only way up, Hyde Street between Chestnut and Bay, was a 20.5 per cent slope under a worn-out pebblestone pavement that waited until 1931 to be rebuilt. The crooked block of Lombard Street was reconstructed in 1994, and by 2019 the Board was writing rules to ration the cars on it. Children raced coaster carts down Leavenworth Street in 1972 and Vallejo Street in 1974, with the Board's written permission. Polk Street along the foot of the hill was given 49 electroliers and 17 electric standards in 1913, and has been closed for its own art fair most summers since the 1970s. Above it the lanes were tidied up one by one — Hastings Place became Hastings Terrace in 1915, a street lamp went up on Macondray in 1919 and in 1948 the Board changed its name from Lane to Street. Until about 1931 it also voted on the fuel oil under each house, fifteen hundred gallons at a time. In 1966 an owner at the bottom of the hill asked to be moved from a forty-foot height limit to two hundred, and was refused. Since the 1970s most of what happens here is a building being cut into flats that sell separately, and the parking measured to the foot between named driveways — but the Board has stopped along the way to name things: the Diego Rivera fresco inside 800 Chestnut Street, a plaque for Tina Modotti outside her family's house on Taylor Street, the Church for the Fellowship of All Peoples on Larkin Street.
